cards.front: Does postfix i++ wait until the end of the statement to change i?
cards.back: No — the variable changes as soon as that subexpression runs; only the old value is handed out
cards.extra: Precedence decides grouping, not delay. JLS 15.14.2: the expression's value is the variable's value before the new value is stored. So in i++ + i, the second i already reads the incremented value. This is why precedence and evaluation order are different questions.
cards.example:
int i = 3;
int j = i++ + i;   // 3 + 4 = 7; i is 4 afterwards

cards.front: With i = 3, what do j and i hold after int j = i++ + i;?
cards.extra: Operands are evaluated left to right: the first i++ yields 3 and immediately stores 4, so the second i reads 4. Compare ++i + i with i=3, which gives 8 (4 + 4).
cards.example:
int i = 3;
int j = i++ + i;   // j=7, i=4
int p = 3;
int q = ++p + p;   // q=8, p=4

cards.back: ++ needs a variable on its left — i * 2 is a value, not an assignable slot
cards.extra: Postfix increment reads a variable, adds one and stores back into that same variable, so its operand must be a variable (an array element or field is fine). javac reports unexpected type: required variable, found value. Writing i++ * 2 is fine because ++ attaches to i first.
cards.example:
int i = 3;
int ok = i++ * 2;   // 6, i becomes 4
int bad = (i * 2)++; // error: required variable, found value
